KEY MESSAGE 1...Heaviest rainfall ending, drier overnight, though 
low clouds and areas of fog are possible. A stray early morning 
shower remains possible too.

The back edge of the heaviest rain is now working from west to east 
across southern New England, with clouds thinning across eastern New 
York and approaching western Massachusetts. Rainfall totals have 
been impressive today, with many areas seeing 2 to 4 inches, mainly 
across Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts. The Flash Flood 
Watch remains in effect through 6 PM. While the heaviest rain is 
over, light to moderate showers linger and could still lead to 
nuisance flooding. Expect these showers to continue for the next 
couple of hours before wrapping up between 4 PM and 6 PM, though a 
few may linger an additional hour or so across the outer Cape.

Drier conditions arrive overnight, though low clouds and areas of 
fog may persist into early Monday morning. A final push of showers 
is possible toward daybreak, though guidance has generally shown 
this activity weakening as it approaches southern New England, 
leaving just a spotty shower or two, mainly in the 4 AM to 8 AM time 
frame. It is worth mentioning that some of the high-resolution 
guidance indicates a bit of a resurgence in shower activity as it 
approaches the coast, possibly picking up on some instability near 
the shore. Nevertheless, this would not lead to impactful weather 
and would be nothing like what we saw today.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry and fall-like Monday into Tuesday, with a chilly 
start Tuesday morning.

Surface high pressure around 1020-1025 mb builds in from the Great 
Lakes region on Monday, settles overhead Monday night, and remains 
with us through Tuesday as a 1030 mb surface high. Little weather to 
talk about during this time frame. While there is lingering moisture 
early Monday morning, with some areas of fog, a much drier airmass 
arrives by noon as PWATs fall below half an inch. 

CAA during the day allows for a period of breezy northwest winds. 
Forecast soundings through BUFKIT show a well-mixed boundary layer 
upwards of 850 mb, which should allow most of the wind aloft to mix 
to the surface. Winds aloft are 25 to 30 kt, resulting in surface 
wind gusts of roughly 20 to 30 mph from the north-northwest. Highs 
Monday afternoon are largely in the lower to middle 70s.

With high pressure overhead Monday night, winds decouple, allowing 
for effective radiational cooling. Have opt'd to do a model blend to 
show the coldest of the guidance. This would mean many of us wake up 
Tuesday morning in the 40s; however, would not be shocked if towns 
in far northwestern Franklin County dip to 38 to 40 degrees. That 
being said, urban centers remain in the upper 40s to lower 50s. 
Boston may retain enough heat due to the urban heat island effect to 
maintain lows in the middle 50s. Lastly, there could be areas of 
ground fog due to the abundant recent rainfall.

Heading into Tuesday, a crisp and dry day with dew points in the 
50s, with some upper 40s possible in northern Massachusetts. 
Meanwhile, 925 mb temperatures settle around +9C to +12C, which 
would suggest high temperatures in the middle 60s to lower 70s. High 
pressure slowly drifts east during the day, with winds shifting to a 
north-northeasterly direction.

KEY MESSAGE 3...High pressure in control next week brings 
generally quiet weather. Brief bout of summer warmth and 
humidity expected Wed- Fri.

High pressure firmly in control by Tuesday will bring much drier 
weather with it. Under dry NW flow dewpoints will be very comfortable 
to start the week, in the 40s. This will be a comfortable taste of 
Fall Tuesday when combined with high temperatures in the upper 60s 
(coasts) to low 70s (inland). As the high shifts over the Atlantic 
Wednesday flow turns southerly bringing the return of more summer-
like temperatures and dewpoints in the upper 70s and mid 60s 
respectively. Still some uncertainty with regard to the forecast for 
late week and next weekend. Zonal mid level flow continues with 
potential for a low to cross somewhere in the vicinity of southern 
New England; whether that stays to our north or goes overhead is 
uncertain, but generally looking at a better shot of unsettled 
weather late Thursday onward.
